topics.title: The Urban Century: 70% by 2050

hook.text: In 2007, more people lived in cities than the countryside for the first time in human history. By 2050, it will be 70%.

buildup.text: That means 2.5 billion more urban residents in 30 years. We need to build the equivalent of a new city every week.

discovery.text: Most growth will happen in Africa and Asia — Lagos, Dhaka, and Kinshasa could each hold 30 million people by mid-century.

twist.text: These cities are growing faster than they can build infrastructure. Many new residents arrive in informal settlements.

climax.text: How these cities grow — planned or chaotic, dense or sprawling — will determine the planet's environmental future.

punchline.text: A new city every week for 30 years. That's the challenge ahead.

quiz.question: What percentage of the world population will live in cities by 2050?

topics.title: Megacities: When a City Hits 10 Million

hook.text: In 1950, only two megacities existed: New York and Tokyo. Today there are 33. By 2030, there will be 43.

buildup.text: A megacity has 10 million or more residents. Tokyo is the largest at 37 million — bigger than most countries.

discovery.text: Megacities produce 60% of global GDP but also 70% of carbon emissions. They are engines of both wealth and pollution.

twist.text: The fastest-growing megacities are in the Global South where governance and infrastructure lag far behind population growth.

climax.text: Managing megacities requires new governance models — regional coordination, metro authorities, and digital infrastructure.

punchline.text: A city bigger than most countries. Governed like a small town. That's the problem.

quiz.question: How many megacities exist today?

topics.title: Shrinking Cities: When People Leave

hook.text: Detroit lost 65% of its population since 1950. Entire neighborhoods are empty — houses abandoned, streets overgrown.

buildup.text: Deindustrialization, suburban flight, and racial tension hollowed out American Rust Belt cities in the late 20th century.

discovery.text: Shrinking cities face a death spiral: fewer residents mean less tax revenue, worse services, and more departures.

twist.text: Japan and Germany face shrinking cities from aging populations, not flight. By 2050, Japan's population will drop by 30 million.

climax.text: Some cities are 'right-sizing' — demolishing empty blocks, consolidating services, and planning for a smaller, better city.

punchline.text: Not every city will grow. Some need a plan for shrinking gracefully.

quiz.question: What causes shrinking cities in Japan?
options: Economic collapse and job losses in manufacturing
Aging population and declining birth rates
Climate change making cities uninhabitable

topics.title: Informal Settlements: The Self-Built City

hook.text: One billion people live in informal settlements — neighborhoods built without permits, plans, or public services.

buildup.text: In Nairobi's Kibera, 250,000 people live in one square mile. There are no formal roads, sewers, or electricity connections.

discovery.text: Informal settlements are not temporary. Families build, expand, and improve homes over decades. They are permanent cities.

twist.text: Demolishing slums displaces people without solving the problem. Upgrading them — adding water, roads, and tenure — works better.

climax.text: Medellín upgraded its hillside barrios with cable cars, libraries, and public spaces. Crime dropped. Property values rose.

punchline.text: They built a city with no help. Imagine what they could do with some.

quiz.question: What is more effective than demolishing informal settlements?
options: Relocating all residents to new apartment towers
Upgrading them with water, roads, and legal land tenure
Replacing them with commercial developments that create jobs

topics.title: Remote Work and the Death of the Office District

hook.text: Post-COVID, office vacancy in US downtowns hit 20%. San Francisco's Financial District lost a third of its weekday foot traffic.

buildup.text: Cities designed around commuting face an existential question: what happens to downtown if no one commutes?

discovery.text: Property taxes on office buildings fund city budgets. Empty offices mean less revenue for schools, police, and transit.

twist.text: Converting offices to apartments is extremely difficult — floor plates are too deep, plumbing is wrong, and zoning forbids it.

climax.text: Cities that diversify downtown — adding housing, culture, and parks — will survive. Mono-use office districts won't.

punchline.text: We built downtown for commuters. Now they work from home. What now?

quiz.question: Why is converting empty offices to apartments difficult?
options: Office leases prevent conversion until they expire in 30 years
Floor plates are too deep, plumbing is wrong, and zoning forbids it
Office buildings are structurally unable to support residential loads

topics.title: Climate Migration: Moving Cities of People

hook.text: By 2050, 1.2 billion people may be displaced by climate change — rising seas, extreme heat, drought, and crop failure.

buildup.text: Small island nations like Tuvalu are already planning evacuations. Miami, Jakarta, and Mumbai face chronic flooding.

discovery.text: Climate migrants will mostly move to cities. Receiving cities need housing, infrastructure, and social services for millions.

twist.text: There is no international legal framework for climate refugees. They have no right to asylum under current law.

climax.text: Cities that plan for climate migration now — building capacity and welcoming newcomers — will thrive. Others will be overwhelmed.

punchline.text: 1.2 billion people will need a new home. No one has planned where.

quiz.question: Why is climate migration a legal challenge?
options: Countries have banned all immigration due to overcrowding
There is no international legal framework recognizing climate refugees
Climate migrants are required to return once conditions improve

topics.title: Sea Level Rise: Cities Underwater

hook.text: If seas rise one meter by 2100, 150 million people will live below the high-tide line. Shanghai, Miami, and Dhaka face inundation.

buildup.text: Coastal cities hold $3 trillion in assets at risk. Flooding will destroy property, infrastructure, and entire economies.

discovery.text: The Netherlands has held back the sea for centuries with dikes, barriers, and water management. Their expertise is in high demand.

twist.text: Some cities can't be protected. Jakarta is sinking and flooding so badly that Indonesia is building a new capital from scratch.

climax.text: Managed retreat — abandoning low-lying areas permanently — is the option no politician wants to discuss. But physics demands it.

punchline.text: The sea doesn't negotiate. It rises. You adapt, or you move.

quiz.question: Why is Indonesia building a new capital city?
options: The current capital is too far from natural resources
Jakarta is sinking and flooding beyond what can be fixed
The government wants to stimulate economic growth in a new region

topics.title: Urban Heat Islands: Cities That Cook

hook.text: Cities are 5-10°F hotter than surrounding countryside. Concrete and asphalt absorb heat. Air conditioning pumps more heat out.

buildup.text: In Phoenix, summer nights stay above 90°F because buildings release stored heat all night. People die in their homes.

discovery.text: Heat kills more Americans than hurricanes, floods, and tornadoes combined. It's the deadliest weather event, and it's invisible.

twist.text: Poor neighborhoods are hotter than wealthy ones. Redlined areas with fewer trees can be 15°F warmer than leafy suburbs.

climax.text: Cool roofs, tree canopy expansion, and reflective pavements can reduce urban heat by 5°F — enough to save hundreds of lives.

punchline.text: The rich live under trees. The poor live on asphalt. In a heat wave, that's life or death.

quiz.question: Why are poor neighborhoods hotter than wealthy ones?
options: Poor neighborhoods use more air conditioning, generating waste heat
Historically redlined areas have fewer trees and more heat-absorbing surfaces
Wealthy neighborhoods are built at higher elevations with cooler temperatures

topics.title: Net-Zero Cities: Eliminating Carbon

hook.text: Cities produce 70% of global carbon emissions. If cities don't go net-zero, the climate crisis can't be solved.

buildup.text: Net-zero means a city's total emissions equal the carbon it removes. It requires electrifying buildings, transit, and industry.

discovery.text: Copenhagen aims to be the first carbon-neutral capital by 2025 — using wind power, bike infrastructure, and district heating.

twist.text: Most net-zero pledges exclude 'embodied carbon' — emissions from making concrete, steel, and asphalt used to build the city.

climax.text: True net-zero requires rethinking construction — using timber, recycled materials, and designing buildings that last centuries.

punchline.text: The city runs on clean energy. But the concrete it's made from heated the planet.

quiz.question: What do most net-zero city pledges fail to include?
options: Emissions from residential heating and cooling systems
Embodied carbon from manufacturing construction materials
Carbon from food production and distribution within the city

topics.title: Flood-Resilient Design: Living with Water

hook.text: The Dutch don't fight water — they live with it. Room for the River gave floodplains back to rivers instead of building walls.

buildup.text: Room for the River lowered levees, widened channels, and created flood parks that absorb water during storms.

discovery.text: The program cost $2.3 billion but protects 4 million people. Flood parks double as recreation areas in dry weather.

twist.text: Most cities still fight water with walls. New Orleans rebuilt the same levees after Katrina. Houston added little after Harvey.

climax.text: China's sponge city program installs permeable surfaces, rain gardens, and wetlands to absorb urban flooding naturally.

punchline.text: Stop fighting the water. Give it somewhere to go.

quiz.question: What was the Dutch 'Room for the River' approach?
options: Building higher sea walls along the entire coastline
Giving floodplains back to rivers instead of fighting water with walls
Pumping river water into underground storage during storms

topics.title: Fire-Adapted Cities: The Wildfire Frontier

hook.text: The 2018 Camp Fire destroyed 19,000 structures in Paradise, California in four hours. The entire town burned.

buildup.text: The wildland-urban interface — where suburbs meet wilderness — is the fastest-growing land use type in America.

discovery.text: Developers build in fire zones because land is cheap and views are beautiful. Homebuyers don't understand the risk.

twist.text: Insurance companies are abandoning fire-prone areas. State Farm and Allstate stopped writing new policies in California.

climax.text: Fire-adapted design uses ember-resistant vents, non-combustible siding, and defensible space. But not building there is safest.

punchline.text: Beautiful views. Cheap land. Until it burns. Then no insurance.

quiz.question: Why are insurance companies leaving fire-prone California areas?
options: California regulations cap insurance premiums below profitable levels
Wildfire risk has increased so much that insuring homes is financially unsustainable
Too few homes in fire zones make the market too small for large insurers

topics.title: Extreme Heat Plans: Cooling the City

hook.text: Miami appointed the world's first Chief Heat Officer in 2021. Her job: keep the city from killing its residents with heat.

buildup.text: Heat action plans include cooling centers, hydration stations, shade structures, and employer protections for outdoor workers.

discovery.text: Ahmedabad, India created the first heat action plan after 1,300 died in a 2010 heat wave. Early warning systems saved thousands.

twist.text: Air conditioning creates a cruel paradox: it cools the inside but heats the outside. More AC means hotter streets.

climax.text: Passive cooling — white roofs, shade trees, cross-ventilation — cuts heat without energy. Ancient techniques beat modern tech.

punchline.text: The city has a Chief Heat Officer. That tells you how bad it's getting.

quiz.question: Why does air conditioning worsen urban heat?
options: AC units consume electricity from fossil fuel plants that emit heat
AC cools interiors but dumps waste heat outside, raising street temperatures
The refrigerants used in AC destroy the ozone layer, increasing UV heating

topics.title: The 15-Minute City: Everything Nearby

hook.text: Imagine reaching work, school, shopping, healthcare, and parks within a 15-minute walk or bike ride. Paris is building this.

buildup.text: Carlos Moreno proposed the concept: every neighborhood should offer all essential services within 15 minutes of every resident.

discovery.text: Paris is converting roads to bike lanes, adding neighborhood markets, and turning schoolyards into public parks on weekends.

twist.text: Conspiracy theorists claimed the 15-minute city is a plot to restrict movement. The concept became a culture war flashpoint.

climax.text: Medieval cities were naturally 15-minute cities. The concept isn't radical — it's a return to what worked for centuries.

punchline.text: Everything you need, 15 minutes away. We had this. Then we invented sprawl.

quiz.question: Who proposed the 15-minute city concept?
options: Jane Jacobs in her work on American cities
Carlos Moreno as a model for Parisian urban reform
Jan Gehl in his studies of Copenhagen street life

topics.title: Car-Free Districts: Reclaiming Streets

hook.text: Vauban in Freiburg, Germany is a car-free neighborhood of 5,500 residents. Streets belong to children, cyclists, and walkers.

buildup.text: Residents can own a car but must park it in a garage at the neighborhood edge. Inside, no cars are allowed on streets.

discovery.text: Car ownership in Vauban is 150 per 1,000 residents — compared to 800 per 1,000 in typical US suburbs.

twist.text: Property values in car-free neighborhoods are higher than car-dependent ones. People pay a premium for quiet, safe streets.

climax.text: Barcelona's superblocks close interior streets to through-traffic, creating car-free plazas in every few blocks.

punchline.text: Remove the cars. The street becomes a park. Property values go up.

quiz.question: What happens to property values in car-free neighborhoods?
options: They decrease because residents can't park near their homes
They increase because people pay a premium for quiet, safe streets
They stay the same because car access doesn't affect property values

topics.title: Floating Cities: Building on Water

hook.text: UN-Habitat endorsed a floating city prototype in 2019. As seas rise, living on water may become a necessity, not a novelty.

buildup.text: BIG architects designed Oceanix City — modular floating platforms housing 10,000 people with solar, farming, and aquaculture.

discovery.text: The Maldives is building the world's first floating city — 5,000 homes on linked platforms in a warm lagoon.

twist.text: Floating cities face huge challenges: sewage, storms, territorial waters, and governance. No nation has legal frameworks for them.

climax.text: Amsterdam already has floating neighborhoods. The technology exists. The question is whether political will matches sea levels.

punchline.text: The sea is rising. Maybe we should learn to float.

quiz.question: Which country is building the world's first floating city?
options: The Netherlands
The Maldives
Singapore

topics.title: New Cities from Scratch: NEOM and Nusantara

hook.text: Saudi Arabia is building NEOM — a $500 billion city in the desert with a 170-kilometer mirrored line of buildings.

buildup.text: Indonesia is building Nusantara, a new capital city on Borneo, to replace sinking Jakarta. Projected cost: $35 billion.

discovery.text: Egypt's New Administrative Capital is being built 45 kilometers east of Cairo to decongest the ancient city.

twist.text: History shows most planned capitals underperform. Brasília, Naypyidaw, and Abuja struggle with low populations and sterile design.

climax.text: Cities built organically — by millions of decisions — are messy but alive. Cities built by decree are often dead on arrival.

punchline.text: A $500 billion city in the desert. History says good luck with that.

quiz.question: Why do most planned capital cities struggle?
options: They're built too far from natural water sources
Top-down design creates sterile environments that fail to attract organic life
Their governments run out of money before completing construction

topics.title: Eco-Districts: Sustainable Neighborhoods

hook.text: Hammarby Sjöstad in Stockholm turns an old industrial site into a neighborhood that recycles its own water, waste, and energy.

buildup.text: Eco-districts integrate solar panels, green roofs, composting, rainwater harvesting, and car-sharing into neighborhood design.

discovery.text: Hammarby residents produce 50% less carbon than the average Stockholm resident. The design makes sustainability effortless.

twist.text: Eco-districts are often expensive and attract wealthy residents. Sustainability becomes a luxury, not a baseline.

climax.text: The challenge is scaling eco-district principles to entire cities — making green design the default, not the premium option.

punchline.text: The green neighborhood exists. It's just too expensive for most people.

quiz.question: What is the main criticism of eco-districts?
options: They don't actually reduce carbon emissions in practice
They tend to be expensive, making sustainability a luxury for the wealthy
They require too much maintenance for average residents to manage

topics.title: Adaptive Reuse: Old Buildings, New Lives

hook.text: The Tate Modern was a power station. The High Line was a freight railway. The best urban spaces are often repurposed ruins.

buildup.text: Adaptive reuse converts obsolete buildings — factories, churches, warehouses — into housing, offices, and cultural spaces.

discovery.text: Reusing buildings saves 50-75% of embodied carbon compared to demolishing and rebuilding. The greenest building already exists.

twist.text: Zoning and building codes often make reuse harder than demolition. Converting a factory to housing can take years of approvals.

climax.text: As cities face climate targets, preserving existing buildings becomes an environmental imperative, not just nostalgia.

punchline.text: The greenest building is the one already standing. Don't demolish it — reimagine it.

quiz.question: Why is adaptive reuse environmentally important?
options: Old buildings are more energy-efficient than new construction
Reusing buildings saves 50-75% of embodied carbon versus rebuilding
Historic buildings generate tourism revenue that funds green initiatives

topics.title: Participatory Planning: Citizens Design the City

hook.text: In Porto Alegre, Brazil, residents directly decide how the city spends its budget. It's called participatory budgeting.

buildup.text: Citizens attend assemblies, propose projects, and vote on priorities. Neighborhoods compete for funding based on need.

discovery.text: Since Porto Alegre started in 1989, over 3,000 cities worldwide have adopted participatory budgeting.

twist.text: Only 2-5% of residents typically participate. The most engaged are often educated, wealthy, and already powerful.

climax.text: Digital platforms are making participation easier. Seoul lets residents propose and vote on projects via smartphone.

punchline.text: Give people a vote on the budget. They spend it on parks and sidewalks, not stadiums.

quiz.question: What is participatory budgeting?
options: A tax system where citizens choose which services their taxes fund
A process where residents directly vote on how city budgets are spent
A crowdfunding platform where citizens donate to city projects

topics.title: Right to the City: Who Belongs?

hook.text: Henri Lefebvre declared in 1968 that every person has a 'right to the city' — to inhabit, use, and shape urban space.

buildup.text: The right to the city means more than living there. It means having power over decisions that shape your neighborhood.

discovery.text: Gentrification, displacement, and exclusionary zoning violate this right by pushing out long-term residents.

twist.text: Brazil enshrined the right to the city in its 2001 City Statute — a law requiring social function of urban property.

climax.text: The New Urban Agenda, adopted by the UN in 2016, recognizes the right to the city as a framework for inclusive planning.

punchline.text: The city belongs to everyone who lives in it. Not just those who own it.

quiz.question: Who coined the phrase 'right to the city'?
options: Jane Jacobs in 1961
Henri Lefebvre in 1968
Carlos Moreno in 2016

topics.title: City Networks: Mayors Leading Where Nations Won't

hook.text: When Trump pulled the US out of the Paris Climate Agreement, 400 American mayors pledged to meet its targets anyway.

buildup.text: City networks like C40, ICLEI, and the Global Covenant of Mayors let cities collaborate on climate, health, and migration policy.

discovery.text: C40 cities represent 700 million people and 25% of global GDP. Acting together, they rival national governments in influence.

twist.text: Cities lack sovereign authority. They depend on nations for funding, regulation, and legal power. Ambition outpaces authority.

climax.text: Urban diplomacy is growing. Mayors meet at the UN, negotiate with businesses, and set standards that nations won't.

punchline.text: Nations debate. Cities act. The mayors aren't waiting for permission.

quiz.question: What is C40?
options: A group of 40 countries committed to carbon reduction
A network of major cities collaborating on climate action
A UN committee overseeing urban development standards

topics.title: Universal Basic Services: Free Transit, Free Water

hook.text: Luxembourg made all public transit free in 2020. Buses, trams, and trains — zero fare for everyone, residents and visitors.

buildup.text: Universal basic services extend the idea beyond transit — free water, sanitation, internet, and public space for all residents.

discovery.text: Vienna offers nearly free public housing, subsidized childcare, and world-class transit for $1 a day. Life quality is superb.

twist.text: Free transit doesn't automatically increase ridership. People also need frequency, coverage, and safety to switch from cars.

climax.text: Universal basic services cost less than universal basic income and deliver more. They target the essentials directly.

punchline.text: Free transit. Free water. A city that works for everyone. Not impossible — Vienna does it.

quiz.question: Which country made all public transit completely free?
options: Austria
Luxembourg
Estonia

topics.title: Land Value Taxation: Taxing Location, Not Buildings

hook.text: Property tax punishes you for improving your building. Land value tax does the opposite — it taxes the land, not what's on it.

buildup.text: Economist Henry George proposed taxing land value in 1879. Land gains value from community investment, not the owner's effort.

discovery.text: Under LVT, an empty lot in downtown pays the same tax as a skyscraper next door. It penalizes speculation and rewards development.

twist.text: LVT has near-universal support among economists. Yet almost no city uses it because landowners have enormous political power.

climax.text: Harrisburg, Pennsylvania shifted to land value tax and saw vacant lots developed, buildings restored, and blight reversed.

punchline.text: Tax the land, not the building. Watch the empty lots fill up overnight.

quiz.question: Why do economists support land value taxation?
options: It generates more revenue than traditional property taxes
It penalizes speculation and rewards productive development of land
It's easier to calculate than assessments based on building value

topics.title: Digital Democracy: Citizens Online

hook.text: Taiwan's vTaiwan platform lets citizens debate policy online. AI clusters opinions to find consensus, not just majority.

buildup.text: Pol.is — the tool behind vTaiwan — maps agreement visually. It shows where opposing sides actually overlap.

discovery.text: Taiwan used the platform to regulate Uber. Both taxi drivers and riders found common ground digitally.

twist.text: Online deliberation can be gamed by bots and organized groups. Verification and moderation are critical.

climax.text: Audrey Tang, Taiwan's Digital Minister, proved that tech can deepen democracy — not just speed it up.

punchline.text: Democracy is slow. Digital tools make it smarter, not just faster.

quiz.question: How does Taiwan's vTaiwan platform build consensus among citizens?
options: By simple majority voting on proposed legislation
By using AI to cluster opinions and find areas of overlap between groups
By selecting random citizens to serve as a deliberative jury

topics.title: Biophilic Cities: Nature in Every Block

hook.text: Singapore puts forests on skyscrapers, parks on highway roofs, and gardens on every available surface. It's a city in a garden.

buildup.text: Biophilic design integrates nature into every building and street — not as decoration, but as essential infrastructure.

discovery.text: Research shows access to nature reduces stress, improves mental health, lowers blood pressure, and increases productivity.

twist.text: Most cities treat nature as optional — a park here, a tree there. Biophilic cities make it mandatory and everywhere.

climax.text: Singapore requires developers to replace greenery removed during construction with equal or greater green space on the building.

punchline.text: Build a tower. Put a forest on top. Singapore says that's not optional.

quiz.question: What does Singapore require of developers who remove greenery?
options: A financial payment to the city's park maintenance fund
Replacement of removed greenery with equal or greater green space on the building
Planting trees in a different neighborhood to offset the loss

topics.title: Child-Friendly Cities: Designing for Kids

hook.text: In 1970, 80% of British children walked to school. Today it's under 40%. Streets became too dangerous for children.

buildup.text: Car-centric cities push children indoors. Traffic danger, pollution, and lack of play space limit their independence.

discovery.text: UNICEF's Child-Friendly Cities Initiative designs urban spaces where children can walk, play, and explore safely.

twist.text: A city safe enough for an eight-year-old to walk alone is safe enough for everyone. Children are the ultimate design test.

climax.text: Bogotá closes 75 miles of streets every Sunday for Ciclovía. Families reclaim roads for cycling, skating, and walking.

punchline.text: If a child can't walk to school safely, the city has failed its most basic test.

quiz.question: Why are child-friendly cities better for everyone?
options: Children generate economic activity that benefits local businesses
A city safe enough for a child to walk alone is safe and accessible for all ages
Child-friendly regulations reduce construction costs for developers

topics.title: Age-Friendly Cities: Designing for Aging

hook.text: By 2050, 2 billion people will be over 60. Most cities are designed for young, able-bodied drivers. That's a problem.

buildup.text: Seniors need walkable streets, accessible transit, nearby healthcare, and social spaces. Suburban sprawl isolates them.

discovery.text: The WHO's Age-Friendly Cities network designs for aging — benches every 100 meters, wide sidewalks, and senior-accessible housing.

twist.text: In car-dependent suburbs, seniors who can't drive become prisoners in their own homes. They lose independence overnight.

climax.text: Dense, walkable, transit-rich neighborhoods are naturally age-friendly. The best city for a senior is the best city for everyone.

punchline.text: Design for the oldest resident. Everyone benefits.

quiz.question: Why does suburban sprawl harm elderly residents?
options: Suburban property taxes are too high for fixed-income seniors
Car-dependent design isolates seniors who can no longer drive safely
Suburban homes are too large for elderly residents to maintain

topics.title: Third Places: Neither Home Nor Work

hook.text: Ray Oldenburg coined 'third place' — the café, barbershop, library, or pub where community happens between home and work.

buildup.text: Third places are free or cheap, welcoming to all, and serve as living rooms for the neighborhood. They build social capital.

discovery.text: Sprawl destroyed third places. Strip malls, drive-throughs, and gated communities replaced the village square.

twist.text: Social media promised virtual third places. Instead, loneliness increased. Online spaces can't replace physical ones.

climax.text: Cities investing in libraries, community centers, and public markets are rebuilding third places. Seoul's book streets thrive.

punchline.text: Not home. Not work. The place where you actually feel like you belong.

quiz.question: What is a 'third place' according to Ray Oldenburg?
options: A third home purchased as a vacation property
An informal gathering spot like a café or library between home and work
A backup workspace used when the office is closed

topics.title: The City of 2100: What Will It Look Like?

hook.text: By 2100, 10 billion people will share the planet. 8 billion will live in cities. What will those cities look like?

buildup.text: Climate adaptation will reshape skylines. Buildings will generate energy, capture carbon, and grow food on their walls.

discovery.text: Autonomous vehicles will eliminate parking — freeing 30% of urban land for housing, parks, and public space.

twist.text: The biggest change won't be technology. It will be governance — who decides how cities grow, and for whom.

climax.text: The best cities of 2100 will be the ones that learned from every mistake described in this course. The worst will repeat them.

punchline.text: We know what works. Parks, transit, density, equity. The future city is a choice.

quiz.question: What will be the most important factor shaping cities by 2100?
options: Which technology becomes dominant for transportation and energy
Governance — who decides how cities grow and who they serve
How many people the planet can physically accommodate

topics.title: Public Space Revival

hook.text: COVID emptied offices and filled parks. Cities realized public space was their most valuable infrastructure.

buildup.text: Open streets, expanded sidewalk dining, and pop-up plazas transformed car lanes into community gathering spaces.

discovery.text: Barcelona's superblocks reclaim nine-block grids from cars, creating playgrounds and gardens on former roads.

twist.text: Privatized public spaces — like malls pretending to be plazas — ban loitering, protests, and homeless people.

climax.text: Cities that invest in genuine public space see lower crime, better health, and stronger social bonds.

punchline.text: The best public space is the one where nobody checks your ID.

quiz.question: What problem do privatized public spaces create in cities?
options: They charge admission fees that exclude low-income residents
They restrict activities like loitering and protests, limiting genuine public use
They close at night, leaving neighborhoods without safe gathering spaces
